plain.li:
[po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences] Come sit and hear a traveller's tale,
for the road is long and the night is cold;
I walked from the hills to the edge of the sea
with a coat too thin and a heart too bold.

I traded my boots for a basket of bread,
I traded the bread for a song in the rain,
I traded the song for a place by a fire,
and I never once wished for my boots again.

So if ever you see a stranger come walking
with nothing to sell and a story to tell,
put a chair by the hearth and a bowl in their hands,
for they have walked the road, and the road has walked them as well.

[po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences,!w:tribal] The river rose in the month of rain,
and it rose a hand each hour,
and the miller's daughter climbed the wheel
to stand above the flour.

She called the town to the high mill floor,
the young, the old, the lame,
and they sat on sacks while the water roared
and sang to keep from shame.

They sang the old songs and the new,
they sang them loud and long,
and when the morning came up grey
the river heard the song.

It bowed its back and it went away,
as rivers sometimes do,
and the miller's daughter climbed back down
and swept the floor anew.

[po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences] He rode out with the raiders at the turning of the year,
with a sword he had not paid for and a grin from ear to ear;
he came back in the springtime with the sword and not the grin,
and he sat down by his mother's door and would not come in.

They asked him what he'd taken, and he told them what he'd lost,
and he named the towns behind him, and he counted up the cost,
and the young ones who were listening went quietly to bed,
and not one of them rode out that year, or so the old ones said.

[po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences] There was a girl who kept the bees
up where the clover grows,
and every spring she spoke to them
the way a keeper knows.

She told them who was born that year,
she told them who had died,
she told them who had married whom
and who had stood beside.

And when she died, the bees were told,
by the youngest of her kin,
and the hives went quiet for a day,
and then they hummed again.

[po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences,theirs] At {TOWN} there is a lamp that burns
all night beside the gate,
for anyone who's coming home
and finds that they are late.

It burned for soldiers, burned for wives,
for children lost and found,
for travellers with nowhere else,
for strays and for the drowned.

And if you ever pass that way
when all the town's asleep,
the lamp will burn for you as well;
that is a promise that we keep.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:spring] The thaw has come, the mud is deep,
the lambs are loud, and nobody sleeps;
the fields are wet, the roads are worse,
and I have written you this verse.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:autumn] The leaves come down, the stores go up,
the {ANIMALS} fatten, and so do we;
the evenings close like a folding hand
round a fire, and a pot, and company.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:winter] The snow is on the roof again,
and on the road, and on the hill;
we keep the fire, we keep the door,
we keep each other, and we keep still.

[po:verse,!condolences,warmly] Between your fire and mine
are hills and weather and a winding line
of road, and every letter goes
the long way round, the way the river flows.
But it arrives. That is the thing.
It always does. And so I sing.

[po:verse,!condolences] I planted a {PLANT} by the door
to see if it would grow;
it did, and now it blocks the door,
and I have to go round, and slow.

[po:verse,!condolences] A letter is a little house
you carry in your hand,
with someone sitting by the fire
in it, from another land.

[po:verse,!condolences,w:spacer] The light from that star left before I was born,
it crossed the long dark without stopping to rest;
it will never arrive at the far end of the sky,
it arrives only here, at my window, a guest.

So when you look up from your side of the hills
and you find the same star, with your letter begun,
remember it's old, and it travelled for you,
and it shines on us both, and it does not mind sharing the one.

[po:verse,!condolences,w:industrial|w:spacer] The lamps hum low on the factory floor,
the clock hands crawl to four;
I've counted the bolts and I've counted the hours,
and I'm counting them still, and more.

But the shift will end and the sun will rise
on the roofs and the wires and the rain,
and I'll walk home with the light in my eyes,
and come back tonight again.

[po:verse,!condolences,empire,warm|cordial] At court the candles never fail,
the floors are glass, the walls are gold;
the music never quite begins,
the soup is never hot, nor ever cold.

I would not change it for the world.
I tell myself so every night.
And then I read your letter, friend,
and wonder if I have it right.

[po:verse,!condolences,ours] At {COLONY} the evenings are long,
and somebody always has a song,
and somebody always has a complaint,
and somebody's always out of paint.

But the roof holds up and the fire holds in,
and we're all of us here, and that's a win;
so here's a verse from our side of the hill,
from all of us here, who are here still.

[po:lament,grave] We laid them down where the {TREE} stands
and the ground is soft in the rain;
we gave them back to the patient land
that gives us all again.

We will not say that they are sleeping,
for they would laugh at that;
we will say they did their share of the work
and left us where they sat.

And when the wind comes over the hill
and the long grass bends and sighs,
we will set a place at the table still,
and look away, and dry our eyes.

[po:lament,grave] There is a chair that no one takes,
a coat still on the peg,
a cup that someone always makes
and no one drinks. I beg

the days to hurry, and they don't;
the nights to pass, and they stay.
I say I'll mend, and think I won't,
and will, one day.

[po:lament,grave,warm|cordial] I cannot carry what you carry,
I cannot walk the road you walk;
but I can sit beside you, quietly,
and need no talk.

And when you are ready, I will listen,
and when you are not, I will wait;
the lamp is lit, the kettle's on,
and it is never late.

[po:lament,grave,!len:short] The bell rang once at morning,
the bell rang once at noon,
the bell rang once at evening
under a thin grey moon.

We counted all the ringing,
we counted all the lost,
we counted every candle
and every winter's frost.

And when the counting's over
and all the names are said,
we'll ring the bell for the living
as we rang it for the dead.

[po:drinking,light,!p:sober] Fill up the cup and pass it along,
the night is short and the ale is strong;
the roof may leak and the fire may smoke,
but the cup goes round, and so does the joke.

Fill up the cup, it's a long way home,
the road is dark and the moon's gone to roam
off with the clouds like a dog with a bone;
so fill up the cup: you won't drink alone.

[po:drinking,light,!p:sober] There's one barrel left and the winter is long,
so we'll drink it in measures and stretch it with song:
a sip for the harvest, a sip for the rain,
a sip for the neighbours who won't come again,
a sip for the goat, who has done nothing wrong,
and the rest for the singer who sings the last song.

[po:drinking,light,!p:sober,!len:short] Oh, the brewer had a cellar and the cellar had a door,
and the door had a key, and the key was on the floor,
and the floor was in the dark, and the dark was full of rats,
and the rats were very drunk, and they were wearing little hats.

Oh, the brewer went down with a lantern in his hand,
and the rats struck up a waltz with a fiddle and a band,
and the brewer said, well, bother it, there's no use in being sour,
and he danced with them till morning, and was sober by the hour.

[po:hymn,c:pious] Before the dawn, before the bread,
before the work and the weather,
we give our thanks for those who wake
and those who sleep, together.

Keep watch on the road and the river and field,
keep watch on the ones we hold near;
and if there is grace left over to give,
we would not mind some here.

[po:hymn,c:pious,!condolences] Praise to {DEITY} in the morning,
praise in the heat of the day,
praise when the lamps are lit at evening
and the children have finished their play.

Praise when the harvest is gathered,
praise when the harvest is thin;
the door of {DEITY}'s hall is open,
and all who are weary come in.

[po:hymn,c:nature] The tree does not ask to be thanked,
the river does not keep score;
the hill gives the hawk its wind for free,
and the sea asks nothing of the shore.

So we will take what we need, and no more,
and mend what we take with care,
and walk on the earth as a guest might walk
through a friend's home, gently, there.

[po:hymn,c:together,!condolences] One hand can lift a cup,
two hands can lift a beam,
a hundred hands can lift a roof,
a thousand lift a dream.

So give me your hand at the harvest,
and give me your hand in the snow,
and I'll give you mine when the road is long,
and wherever you go.

[po:work,c:herd,!condolences] Walk on, my slow ones, walk on easy,
the grass is sweet on the farther hill;
the sky is wide and the wind is breezy,
and the road is long, and there's time to kill.

Walk on, my slow ones, the river's waiting,
the evening's soft and the fire is near;
there's nobody chasing and nobody hating,
and nobody hurrying anyone here.

[po:work,!condolences,!w:tribal] Cut the corn and bind the sheaf,
the sun is hot and the day is brief;
one for the barn and one for the mill,
one for the birds on the windowsill,
and one for the one who works the least,
so they'll be quiet at the harvest feast.

[po:war,c:raider|c:martial,!condolences] Sharpen the blade on the long winter night,
mend the strap and the shield and the boot;
when the snow goes, the road will be ours by right,
and we'll come home heavy with loot.

Drink to the ones who will ride at our side,
and to those who rode out and did not come back;
the fire burns high and the hall is wide,
and we leave their cups where they hung, on the rack.

[po:nonsense,light] A goat went to market to buy a new hat,
and came back with a cabbage, a shovel, a cat;
the cat ate the cabbage, the shovel ran off,
and the goat wore the hat to a dance, with a cough.

[po:nonsense,light] There once was a cook at the edge of a town
who made a great pudding, three storeys and brown;
it stood in the square for a fortnight or more,
till {ANANIMAL} came by and went in at the door.

[po:nonsense,light] I asked the moon to dinner,
the moon said she was full;
I asked the sun to supper,
the sun said it was dull;
I asked the stars to breakfast,
they came, and stayed till noon,
and ate up all the porridge,
and never asked the moon.

[po:nonsense,light] My uncle kept a turnip that could whistle in the dark;
it whistled at the neighbours and it whistled at the lark,
it whistled at the weddings and it whistled at the dead,
until somebody boiled it, and we had soup instead.

[po:song,w:tribal] The fire is old. The fire is warm.
It was here before the hunt.
It will be here after the hunt.
Sit by it. Tell it your name.

The fire knows the names of the dead.
It says them in the smoke.
Watch the smoke go up.
Do not be afraid. It is only remembering.

[po:song,w:tribal,!condolences] Rain on the hide, rain on the stone,
rain on the old ones' bones;
the grass drinks, the {ANIMALS} drink,
the river grows, and the people sing.

[po:song,w:tribal] Feet, carry me.
Sky, cover me.
Path, know me.
Fire at the end of it, wait for me.

[olde,po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences] Come list, and I will tell thee true
how once the waters rose,
and how the miller's daughter stood
where yet the alder grows.

She called the town unto the mill,
the young, the old, the lame,
and they did sit upon the sacks
and sing to keep from shame.

And when the grey morn came at last
the river heard the song,
and bowed its back and went its way,
for it had stayed too long.

[olde,po:ballad,!len:short,!condolences] A knight rode out from the castle gate
with a lance and a borrowed horse,
to win the hand of a lady fair
and a purse of gold, of course.

He fought a bear, he fought a bull,
he fought a man in black,
and every time he won the fight
he lost the purse, and came back.

And now he keepeth a little farm
with a goat and a borrowed plough,
and the lady fair is wed to the bull,
and the knight is happier now.

[olde,po:verse,!condolences,season:winter] The snow lieth deep upon the wold,
the hearth is warm, the night is cold;
Heaven keep thee, friend, where'er thou art,
and keep a corner of thy heart
for us, who sit and think of thee
when the long dark lieth on the lea.

[olde,po:verse,!condolences,season:spring] Now cometh spring with mud and rain,
the lambs are loud, the plough is out;
I think of thee, and think again,
and wonder what thou art about.

[olde,po:verse,!condolences] A letter is a little hall
that one may carry in the hand,
with someone seated by the fire
within it, from another land.

[olde,po:lament,grave] They laid our friend beneath the yew
where the cold rain falleth slow,
and all the folk our friend e'er knew
stood weeping in a row.

Weep not, our friend would say to us,
for rest is come at last;
but set a cup out, even thus,
and drink, when grief is past.

[olde,po:lament,grave,warm|cordial] I may not bear the load thou bearest,
nor walk the road that thou must go;
but I will sit with thee, if thou carest,
and keep the watch till the fire is low.

[olde,po:drinking,light,!p:sober] Bring forth the cup and fill it high,
and let the sorry world go by;
the roof may leak, the rain may fall,
but here is ale enough for all.

Bring forth the cup and fill it full,
the night is long, the day was dull;
and if thou drink'st thy fill and more,
we'll bear thee home, as oft before.

[olde,po:hymn,c:pious] At dawn we praise, at noon we pray,
at eventide we bless
the bread, the roof, the one more day,
and all our neighbours' rest.

[olde,po:hymn,c:pious,!condolences] Praise be to {DEITY} at break of day,
and praise when the sun is high,
and praise when the lamps are lit at eve
and the stars come out in the sky.

[olde,po:nonsense,light] A knight rode forth upon a goose,
his armour made of cheese;
he challenged every man he met,
and fell at every breeze.

[olde,po:work,!condolences] Reap the field and bind the sheaf,
the sun is hot, the day is brief;
one for the lord and one for the mill,
one for the birds upon the sill,
and one for him that laboureth least,
that he be quiet at the feast.

[sv:fey,po:song] By root and ring, by dew and stone,
this song is yours, and yours alone;
sing it once at the edge of night,
and the ring will know you, and treat you right.
By stone and dew, by ring and root,
we close the song, and the song is mute.

[sv:fey,po:song,!condolences] Three hops to the left of the old oak's shadow,
two to the right of the moon on the meadow,
there is a door that is not a door,
and we will be there, as we were before.

[sv:green,po:song] Slow light,
slow root,
the rain comes down
and we drink it, and we are glad.
The sun comes back
and we turn to it,
all of us, together, without hurry.

[sv:green,po:song] A seed is a letter
written to the spring.
We are writing to you
the same way.

[sv:machine,po:verse,!condolences] VERSE 1 OF 1.
THE SUN ROSE AT 0613.
IT WAS ADEQUATE.
I OBSERVED IT FOR FOURTEEN MINUTES,
WHICH WAS NOT REQUIRED.

[sv:machine,po:verse,light] ATTEMPT 7 AT RHYME:
THE RAIN FALLS ON THE ROOF.
THE ROOF IS WATERPROOF.
THIS IS BOTH A FACT AND PROOF.
I AM TOLD THIS SOUNDS ALOOF.

[sv:ancient,po:song] In the old tongue this was sung at the turning of the year, and took a night to sing. I give you the last verse only, which is the part everyone remembered.

Let the cold come; it has come before.
Let the dark come; it has gone before.
We are still at the table.
Pour.

[po:lament,grave,!len:short] Lay the tools down by the door,
the ones the hands won't need;
the seed is in, the field is sown,
and someone else will weed.

Hang the coat upon the peg
where it has always hung;
we'll leave it there a little while,
the way a song is left unsung.

And when the spring comes up the lane
with all its noise and green,
we'll say the name out loud, and then
we'll do the things between.

[po:lament,grave] The kettle sings, the bread still bakes,
the sun comes up the same;
the whole world goes about its work
and never learns the name.

[po:lament,grave,w:tribal] We sang your name to the river,
and the river carried it on;
we sang your name to the fire,
and the fire burned until dawn.

Go where the old ones are walking,
where the grass is long and the herds are near;
leave a track at the edge of the morning,
and we will follow, but not this year.

[po:lament,grave,w:spacer] We sent you up in the shuttle's fire,
the old way, the ship way, the way of the crew;
the stars didn't notice, the stars never do,
but we did, and we do.

[po:lament,grave,w:industrial] The whistle blew at the end of the shift
and everyone came up but one;
we stood in the yard with our caps in our hands
and waited, and the waiting's not done.

[po:lament,grave,their:herders] The herd went up to the high grass
without you walking at the back;
the old cow stopped at the bend of the hill
and looked for you along the track.

[po:lament,grave,empire] The banners hang at half the mast
in every hall of the court;
the heralds read the titles out,
and the list is one name short.

[olde,po:lament,grave] Now is the candle burnt away
that lit thee to thy bed;
now is the long day done, and we
must tell it to the dead.

We keep thy chair beside the hearth,
thy cup upon the shelf;
and if we weep, forgive us that:
thou wouldst have wept thyself.

[olde,po:lament,grave,theirs] The bells of {TOWN} rang slow and low
for one that we did love;
the rooks went up, the rain came down,
the grey sky hung above.

Go softly, friend, the road is long
and thou art weary-shod;
we'll walk with thee unto the gate
and lay thee in the sod.

[olde,po:lament,grave] Here lieth one that mended nets
and would not mend a quarrel;
who never won a single race,
and never wanted laurel.

[olde,po:lament,grave,their:fishers] The river took thee in the dark
and gave thee back at morn;
we laid thee on the landing stage
where first thy boat was borne.

Sleep, waterman, the tide is out,
the nets are hung to dry;
the river saith thy name each night,
and so, each night, do I.

[u:none,po:lament,grave] we put him in the ground
and sed sum wurds
not good wurds
but the best we had

[po:drinking,light,!p:sober,!condolences,w:industrial|w:spacer] Here's to the boss, who is out of the room,
here's to the foreman, who's out of his head,
here's to the shift that is over at last,
and here's to the morning, which waits by the bed.

[po:drinking,light,!p:sober,!condolences,w:spacer] One for the hull and one for the drive,
one for the stars that we left behind,
one for the planet that kept us alive,
and one for the cook, because she's been kind.

[po:drinking,light,!p:sober,!condolences,w:tribal] Pass the skin, the berry wine is sweet,
the fire is high, the drums are at our feet;
tomorrow we hunt and tomorrow we roam,
but tonight the hill is home.

[olde,po:drinking,light,!p:sober,!condolences] Bring in the jug and set it down,
the frost is on the thatch;
the miller's drunk, the reeve's in town,
and none will mind the latch.

So drink to thee and drink to me,
and drink to all the rest,
and last of all unto the cask
that we do love the best.

[olde,po:drinking,light,!p:sober,!condolences] Ale for the reaper and mead for the bride,
wine for the friar, who saith he hath none;
water for horses, and all for the guest,
and naught for the tax-man till all the work's done.

[po:hymn,c:pious,!condolences] {DEITY}, who keeps the lamps alight
when all the world goes dark,
keep watch upon the road tonight
and on the ones who walk.

And if we stray, as strays the sheep,
and if we fall, as falls the rain,
be patient with us while we sleep,
and wake us up again.

[po:hymn,c:pious,!condolences] Morning, and the light comes in
through the gap above the door;
we did not earn it, did not ask,
and it comes in, as before.

Evening, and the light goes out
behind the hill and down the lane;
we thank it for the day it gave,
and trust it will come back again.

[po:hymn,c:nature,!condolences] Old tree, older than our names,
we come to you with open hands;
we take the fallen, not the green,
and leave the root where the root stands.

Rain on the leaf and rain on the stone,
rain on the ones who are not yet grown;
we are the guests, and you are the hall,
and the hall was here before us all.

[po:hymn,c:transhuman,!condolences] Blessed be the steady hand
that sets the wire beneath the skin;
blessed be the better eye
that lets the farther light come in.

The flesh is clay, and clay will crack,
the bone is chalk, and chalk will wear;
but we were made to make ourselves,
and what we make, we can repair.

[po:hymn,c:martial,!condolences,!p:sober] Raise the shield and raise the song,
the hall is warm, the night is long;
the ones who fell are at the board
with a cup in the hand that held the sword.

We'll join them when the time has come,
not before, and not from fear;
till then we keep the fire lit
and drink to them, and drink to here.

[po:hymn,c:together,!condolences] Many hands beneath one roof,
many mouths around one pot;
what one has, the many have,
and what one lacks, the many not.

Sing it at the long table,
sing it in the furrowed field:
none of us is fed till all are,
and that is how a town is healed.

[po:hymn,c:pain,!condolences] The cold is a teacher, the thorn is a friend,
the long road a sermon that comes to no end;
we bless what is bitter, we bless what is hard,
for the soft things forget us, and the hard things keep guard.

[po:hymn,c:dark,!condolences] Put out the lamp, the dark is kind,
it asks for nothing, hides the scars;
the eye that's closed can learn to find
what's lost in all the glare of stars.

[po:hymn,c:sea,!condolences] Tide come in and tide go out,
take the boat and bring it back;
we are yours beyond a doubt,
whether the net is full or slack.

Water give and water take,
water keep us in your hand;
all we are is for your sake,
and what we are is not of land.

[po:hymn,c:herd,!condolences] Bless the herd that walks before us,
bless the dog that walks behind;
bless the grass that waits up yonder,
bless the weather, if it's kind.

[po:hymn,c:peace,!condolences] Lay the spear across the door
and let it gather dust;
the hand that never strikes a blow
is the hand that we can trust.

[po:hymn,c:tunnel,!condolences] Down in the deep where the roots come through,
where the stone is warm and the dark is true,
we dig and we sing and the mountain hears,
and it keeps us safe, as it has for years.

[po:hymn,w:tribal,!condolences] Spirit of the long grass,
spirit of the stone,
we have taken only what was given,
we have left the rest alone.

[olde,po:hymn,c:pious,!condolences] At matins, when the cock doth crow,
and vespers, when the light is low,
we lift our hands, we bend the knee,
and ask a blessing upon thee.

[olde,po:hymn,c:pious,!condolences] O {DEITY}, keep the harvest dry,
and keep the river in its bed;
keep wolf from fold and hawk from sky,
and give us each our daily bread.

[po:verse,empire,!condolences] In the white halls where the fountains play
and the floors are older than the sun,
we bow at the turning of every day
to the one who is owed by everyone.

And I, who am small in the long parade,
a name on a scroll in a gilded case,
would trade the whole of the court's brocade
for an hour of the road to your gate, and your face.

[po:verse,empire,!condolences] Honour is a heavy coat;
it keeps the cold off, keeps you straight,
it fits too tight across the throat,
and someone else decides its weight.

[po:song,empire,!condolences] Sing of the Stellarch, sing of the throne,
sing of the stars that the Empire has known;
sing of the knights who have knelt in the hall,
and sing very softly: the walls hear it all.

[po:ballad,empire,!condolences,!len:short] There was a knight of little land
and less of anything,
who bowed so well, and kissed so well,
the hand of every king.

He bowed his way to baronet,
he bowed his way to count,
and every bow went in a book,
and every book went to account.

And when at last they made him duke
he found, to his surprise,
that all the bows were owed to him,
and none would meet his eyes.

[olde,po:ballad,!condolences,!len:short] The ferryman's daughter of the ford
was fairer than the morn,
and every lad on either bank
would cross, and be forlorn.

For she would take thy penny, aye,
and take thee o'er the stream,
but not a word nor smile at all
for any lad's sweet dream.

Till came a tinker, deaf and old,
that could not hear her scorn,
and talked the whole way over-stream
of kettles, and of corn.

And now they keep the ferry both,
and quarrel night and morn,
and she is happy as a lark,
and he hath never sworn.

[olde,po:ballad,!condolences,!len:short] Old Wat the ringer rang the bell
for births and deaths and weddings too,
and rang it loud for those he loved,
and soft for those he never knew.

He rang for lords, he rang for thieves,
he rang for any that would pay,
and rang it twice for the miller's goat
that wandered home on Lammas day.

And when Old Wat lay down at last
and none was left that knew the rope,
the bell rang once, all by itself,
and all the town looked up in hope.

[olde,po:ballad,!condolences,!len:short] There is a lantern at the cross
where the four roads meet the wood,
and one keeps watch beneath it still,
as the Wardens always should.

And if thou comest late at night
with something at thy back,
run to the light, and do not turn,
and do not leave the track.

For what is in the wood is old,
and what is by the lamp is older;
and one of them would eat thee whole,
and one will set thee on its shoulder.

[olde,po:ballad,!condolences,!len:short] The lord came down to count his sheep
and found one sheep a goat;
he had it seized, he had it tried,
he had it read a note.

The goat it ate the note, my lord,
it ate the lord's own seal,
it ate the hem of the judge's gown
and half the judge's meal.

And now it standeth in the hall
with ribbons on its horn:
the only beast in all the shire
that hath a pardon sworn.

[olde,po:ballad,!condolences] She waited at the orchard wall
the whole of the apple year;
he went to the wars with a borrowed horse,
a promise, and a spear.

The apples budded, the apples fell,
the apples went to cider;
he came back home with a wooden leg,
a wife, and a horse beside her.

[olde,po:song,!condolences,their:pilgrims] We walk, we walk, the road is long,
the shrine is far away;
we sing the same four lines of song
from dawn to close of day.

And when we reach the shrine at last
and kneel upon the stone,
we find we walked the whole way there
to learn we're not alone.

[olde,po:song,!condolences,their:healers] Bring the sick and bring the lame,
bring the ones that have no name;
we ask no coin and ask no creed,
we ask but this: what dost thou need?

[olde,po:song,!condolences,their:sextons] Ring for the morning, ring for the dead,
ring for the bride and the bridal bed;
ring for the stranger that came to the town,
ring for us all when the sun goeth down.

[olde,po:war,!condolences,their:mercenaries] Sign thy name upon the roll
and take thy silver, take thy pike;
the Banner payeth on the nail,
and the Banner's dead are all alike.

We'll write thee down if thou shouldst fall
in the long book with the rest;
the Banner never loseth a name,
and that is what the Banner doth best.

[olde,po:work,!condolences,their:artisans] Clay on the wheel and fire in the kiln,
mark on the bottom and glaze on the brim;
it leaveth our hands and it goeth abroad,
but the mark saith whose, and the mark is our word.

[olde,po:verse,!condolences,season:autumn] The leaves are down, the barns are full,
the swallows gone to warmer lands;
I write to thee by candlelight
with cold and ink upon my hands.

[olde,po:verse,!condolences,fam:familiar|fam:close] I keep thy letters in a chest
that held my grandam's wedding thread;
it shutteth with a little sound,
like one that goeth up to bed.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:winter] The snow has made the town a page
that no one's written on as yet;
the children will be out by noon
to fill it up, and get it wet.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:summer] The bees are drunk on the lime tree,
the dog is asleep in the road;
the whole of the day is a slow thing,
and nobody's carrying a load.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:spring,light] Mud to the ankle, mud to the knee,
lambs in the yard and a frog in the tea;
spring has come back like a cousin who stays,
too loud and too muddy, and we've missed her for days.

[po:verse,!condolences,fam:familiar|fam:close] I keep your letters in a box
that used to hold my mother's thread;
it closes with a little click,
like someone going up to bed.

[po:verse,!condolences,fam:new] To someone I have never met:
the road is long, the ink is wet;
I do not know your face or name,
but here's a verse for you all the same.

[po:verse,!condolences,w:spacer] Up there the ships go over slow,
silver needles on the blue;
someone up there is writing home,
and someone down here's writing too.

[po:verse,!condolences,w:industrial] The mill-race runs, the engines hum,
the stacks put out their smoky thread;
the whole town works the whole night through
so that the whole town can be fed.

[po:work,!condolences,their:drillers] Down goes the bit and up comes the mud,
up comes the water and up comes the crud;
down goes the pay and up go the bills,
and round goes the wheel in the Deepwell hills.

[po:work,!condolences,their:linesmen] Climb the mast and mind the wire,
mind the wind and mind the rust;
someone down the line is talking,
and the line's the line we trust.

[po:work,!condolences,w:tribal] Stone on stone and seed between,
grind it fine and grind it clean;
the sun is high, the work is long,
so the stone gets half the song.

[po:war,!condolences,c:raider] Over the hill when the moon is gone,
down on the wagons before the dawn;
take what is heavy and leave what is slow,
and be over the hill before the cocks crow.

[po:nonsense,light,!condolences] The mayor of the moon came down for tea
and sat on the cat, who objected;
he drank all the milk and he ate all the bread
and left rather sooner than expected.

[po:nonsense,light,!condolences] A pig in a hat and a cow in a coat
went sailing away in a leaky boat;
they sailed for a week and they sailed for a day,
and they're sailing still, or so the pigs say.

[u:none,po:song,!condolences,!nr:head] oh the boss is a big man
and the boss has a big hat
and the boss is in the kichen
and thats the end of that

[po:song,!condolences,their:crew] Hold the line and hold the deck,
the ship is old, the ship's a wreck;
but every bolt is one we know,
and someday, someday, up we go.

[po:song,!condolences,their:seers,light] Red at morning, glass is low,
wind from the west and rain to follow;
the tower sees what the sky will do,
and tells the town, and the town says: so?

[po:song,!condolences,their:traders] Silk for the city and salt for the hills,
iron for anyone paying the bills;
the road is long and the profit is thin,
but the wagon goes out and the wagon comes in.

[po:song,!condolences,their:tamers] Gentle the beast with a hand on the flank,
gentle the beast with a word;
the ring is the place where the two of you learn
which one of you's going to be heard.

[po:song,!condolences,their:salvagers] Rust on the wheel and rust on the hull,
nothing is empty and nothing is full;
what the old world dropped, the Wheel picks up,
and somebody drinks from a stranger's cup.

[po:song,!condolences,their:listeners] Hush, the Spire is humming low,
something in it wants to know;
we sit and listen, row on row,
and some of us hear, and some of us go.

[po:song,!condolences,their:vaultfolk] The door came open after all those years,
and the sun came in like a shout;
we'd learned every song for the dark inside,
and none for the world without.

[po:song,!condolences,their:scholars,light] Shelve it, label it, file it away,
cross-reference everything said today;
somewhere a fact is beginning to fade,
so copy it twice, and be very afraid.

[po:song,!condolences,their:citizens] For the Republic, the bread and the vote,
the meeting that ran till the moon was afloat;
we argued all night and we voted at dawn,
and nobody won, but the motion went on.

[po:song,!condolences,their:mechanitors] Many hands and one mind,
many treads and one road;
the Lattice hums and the Lattice thinks,
and none of us carries the load.

[po:song,!condolences,their:editors] Change the code and change the skin,
change the light the eye lets in;
what you were born is where you start,
and not the whole of the art.

[sv:fey,po:song,!condolences] By leaf, by string, by the hour of dew:
we made a song, and it is for you.
It has no end, so we stop it here,
and it goes on singing for a year.
By dew, by string, by the leaf: it is true.

[sv:fey,po:verse,!condolences] Count the mushrooms in the ring:
one for a wish and two for a king,
three for a debt that is never paid,
four for the bargain you never made.

[sv:fey,po:lament,grave] By ash and by ember, by the last of the light:
one of the ring has gone out of the ring.
We dance with a gap in the circle tonight.
By the light, by the ember, by ash: we sing.

[sv:green,po:lament,grave] One of us has gone to the soil.
This is not sad,
we tell ourselves,
slowly,
all season.

[sv:green,po:song,!condolences,season:spring] Up. Up.
The frost has let go of the root.
Up. Up.
The light has come back for us.
We have waited all winter to say this:
up.

[sv:machine,po:lament,grave] RECORD OF LOSS.
UNIT COUNT: ONE FEWER.
THIS UNIT HAS RUN THE NUMBERS SEVERAL TIMES.
THEY DO NOT IMPROVE.
END OF VERSE.

[sv:machine,po:song,!condolences,light] SONG, ATTEMPT 12:
LA.
LA.
LA IS A NOTE. I AM TOLD THERE ARE OTHERS.
I AM SAVING THEM.

[sv:ancient,po:verse,!condolences] I wrote this in a language that has died.
I have translated it for you, badly.
It says: the river does not remember the boat,
but the boat remembers the river.
It rhymed, once.

[sv:ancient,po:lament,grave] I have buried friends in eleven centuries.
It does not get easier.
It gets quieter.
I have mistaken the quiet for easier, more than once.

[sv:beast,po:song,!condolences] Moon up.
Nose up.
The whole pack sings,
not well,
but all at once,
which is the point.

[sv:beast,po:lament,grave] One track stops at the river.
We walk up and down the bank,
all night,
smelling for the other side.

[sv:hive,po:song,!condolences] We hum.
The cells hum.
The queen hums.
The hum is the song.
The song is us.

[sv:hive,po:lament,grave] One cell is quiet.
We hum around it.
We will hum around it
for a long time.

[sv:deep,po:verse,!condolences] Below the floor of the sea is a floor.
Below that floor, a door.
To the door we sing.
The door, it sings back, more.

[po:verse,!condolences] A letter is a slow thing,
it walks the road on someone's feet;
it stops at inns and takes the rain,
and when it comes, it comes complete.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:winter] Frost on the window, frost on the pail,
frost on the cart in the yard;
I breathe on the glass and write your name,
and the name stays there, small and hard.

[po:verse,!condolences] The bread is rising, the fire is in,
the cat is somewhere she shouldn't be;
the whole of the house is a quiet thing,
and the quietest part of it's me.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:spring] The swallows are back in the barn again
as if they had never been away;
they don't explain and they don't apologise,
which I mean to try myself one day.

[po:verse,!condolences,season:summer] Long day, short night,
the moon just barely in;
the whole town sleeps up on the roofs
and wakes with the sun on its skin.

[po:verse,!condolences,w:tribal] The fire is the oldest friend,
older than the oldest one;
it was here before the stories,
and it listens till they're done.

[po:verse,!condolences,w:industrial] The tram goes by at half past eight,
the bell rings at the gate,
and somewhere in the whole machine
someone is writing, late.

[po:verse,!condolences,w:spacer] Out past the last of the lit windows
the dark goes on for good;
we keep a lamp in the end house
as the old ships said we should.

[olde,po:verse,!condolences] A letter is a little road
that runneth hand to hand;
it stayeth not for rain nor snow,
and cometh where 'tis planned.

[olde,po:verse,!condolences,season:spring] The swallows to the barn are come
as they had never flown;
they make no plea, nor tell their way,
and so the spring is shown.

[po:verse,!condolences,empire] The candles burn in the long gallery,
the portraits watch the floor;
I walk the length of it every night
and think of the world outside the door.

[po:song,!condolences,empire,!len:short,light] Sir Tancred went to the Stellarch's ball
with a borrowed sword and a borrowed shoe;
he bowed to the left, he bowed to the right,
and he bowed to the punch bowl too.

They gave him a title, they gave him a hall,
they gave him a horse and a seat at the fore;
and he never once knew what he'd done to deserve it,
so he went back and bowed some more.

[po:lament,grave,their:crew] We gave them to the dark the old way,
with the ship's book read and the lights turned low;
the stars took them in without a word,
the way the stars take all we know.

[olde,po:lament,grave,their:sextons] Ring once for the cradle and once for the bride,
and once for the one that is laid to rest;
the bell that rang thee into the world
shall ring thee out of it, and ring it best.

[po:hymn,!condolences,their:listeners] Hum of the Spire, low and long,
fill the empty with your song;
we do not know what you are saying,
but we stay, and we keep praying.

[po:song,!condolences,their:tamers,light] My beast is a terror, my beast is a dream,
my beast is a nuisance, my beast is a team;
we've been in the ring every day since the spring,
and my beast has won nothing, and won everything.

[olde,po:song,!condolences,their:fishers,light] Row, row, the river is wide,
and the fish are all on the other side;
row, row, the river is long,
and the fish have heard of us, and are gone.

[olde,po:song,!condolences,their:hunters] Trim the lamp and watch the wood,
the night is long, the light is good;
what walketh out there walketh slow,
and keepeth from the lantern's glow.

[u:none,po:war,!condolences,c:raider] we are the lads from over the hil
we dont pay and we never wil
we take wot we like and we like a lot
and we rote this song. its all we got
